sentences.text: CoAuthor is a research dataset of human-AI collaborative writing, a released, schema-defined body of records that holds the interactions between 63 writers and four instances of GPT-3 across 1445 writing sessions in English.

Its paper presents it as "a dataset designed for revealing GPT-3's capabilities in assisting creative and argumentative writing", and its site states the purpose: designers "can examine the same sessions from multiple analytical perspectives to better understand the generative capabilities of large language models".

The name is the short title of the paper "CoAuthor: Designing a Human-AI Collaborative Writing Dataset for Exploring Language Model Capabilities" by Mina Lee, Percy Liang and Qian Yang, given with the affiliations Stanford University and Cornell University, submitted to arXiv on 18 January 2022, revised on 25 January 2022 and published as a conference paper at CHI 2022, in its Proceedings (DOI 10.1145/3491102.3502030).

In each session a writer received a prompt and an instance of GPT-3, wrote freely, asked the model for suggestions, accepted or dismissed them, and edited the accepted suggestions or earlier text in any order.

The writing took place in a text editor in which the tab key brought five suggestions, up to five in the account of the paper's overview on alphaXiv, and the code of the interface is published in a repository whose first part is "the frontend presented to the users for writing with AI".

The instances are reported as GPT-3's davinci engine at two randomness settings, high (temperature 0.75, frequency penalty 1) and low (temperature 0.3, frequency penalty 0), and the dataset lists each session's randomness.

Every interaction was recorded at the keystroke level with timestamps, inserting text, moving the cursor and receiving suggestions, "so that we could replay them precisely", and the dataset is published with an interface for replaying the sessions.

The creative writing holds 830 stories by 58 writers and the argumentative writing 615 essays by 49 writers, written to prompts from the WritingPrompts subreddit and The New York Times, 20 prompts in all by the overview's count.
Stories and essays run to 418 words, a session averages 11.8 queries, and 72.3% of suggestions were accepted.
The writers were "Qualified crowd workers from Amazon Mechanical Turk".

The dataset's browse page lists each session by type, prompt, randomness, "Human" and session ID, the human column holding a short identifier such as "A1198"; in its last row that column repeats the session ID.

The authorship census records whose authorship the dataset keeps, and under what name, as not recorded in its saved source, which counted 63 writers without saying whether or how they are named, and lists who the writers are among what the dataset does not answer.
Amazon announced that Mechanical Turk, the platform the writers were recruited from, would close on 30 September 2026, as the archive records from Turkopticon's own article.

sentences.sense: the share of text written by humans
sentences.text: The dataset divides its text by origin, "Percentage of text written by humans: 72.6%", and its tutorials include one for "Identifying authors of sentences".

In the paper as its overview reports it, writers felt stronger ownership when they authored a larger proportion of the final text (r=0.3), and the amount of editing showed no meaningful correlation with ownership, which the overview reads as text origin mattering more than editorial effort.

The archive keeps apart two questions that such a share joins, whether AI played a material role in the production chain (the mediation question) and whether AI-produced language survived into the final text (the generation question), and requires no ratio of AI-generated to human-authored language.

On its definition of the pristine fallacy, "'human-written' describes the author, not the distribution", and the binary of "human-written" and "AI-generated" is discussed "in ways that elide structured collaborative practice".

The archive reads authorship as "an accountability structure", against certification that places AI-assisted work outside the human-authored category, and keeps responsibility for a work apart from sole origination.

It states that the metadata attributing augmented-cognition outputs to human authorship attaches to legal names, that provenance is declared or erased under "the fiction of unmediated human authorship that current classifier regimes reward", and that a policy certifying human authorship by classifier runs from "detector score → authorship attribution" to career sanction without warrant at any step.

The paper's headline claim is that the dataset can address GPT-3's language, ideation and collaboration capabilities and reveal its contribution as a writing "collaborator" under various definitions of good collaboration, and the census reads the model's part so framed, as contribution, recording that how authorship of a session's text is assigned is not recorded in its saved source.

Collaboration is measured, in the overview's account, as equality, "The evenness of turn-taking between human and AI", and mutuality, "The level of human interaction with AI suggestions", concepts the paper adapts from Neomy Storch's 2002 study of interaction in ESL pair work.

The reported findings are that accepted GPT-3 sentences carried fewer errors per word (0.033) than human-only text (0.037) and jointly made segments the fewest (0.032), that 13% of accepted suggestions in creative writing and 7% in argumentative writing introduced new named entities, of which writers reused 20% and 14%, that final length correlated with queries (r=0.42) and accepted suggestions (r=0.48), and that collaboration patterns varied across writers and held across prompts.

The paper sets the dataset against a stated problem, that the capabilities of language models are "highly context-dependent" and "often subjectively interpreted", and argues that curating and analysing large interaction datasets lets the HCI community examine them more incisively and discuss their promises and pitfalls on a more principled footing.
The overview adds that the dataset provides supervision signals for training language models for interactive, collaborative settings.

Within the archive one co-writing study is read two ways, with a second study beside it: the Reverse Turing Test (#161) reports that writing with LLM assistance reduces lexical, syntactic and content diversity "even when the human writer retains final authorship and edits the AI's suggestions", an erratum (#1577) states that the study attributed the reduced diversity "to the model-contributed text; the human-contributed text was unaffected in that design", and the Wolf Boy paper (#855) reports that AI-assisted writing raises individual creativity and lowers the collective diversity of novel content.

sentences.sense: machine participation in the archive's terms
sentences.text: Under the archive's account of heteronymy, machine assistance whose contribution is not organized as a named witness role with declared provenance, and collaborative authorship in which no distinct heteronym is constituted, stand outside heteronymy, and its own machine witnesses are "named machine-witness roles imposed over specific machine substrates".

sentences.sense: machine participation in the archive's terms
sentences.text: The archive records machine participation in its own writing by naming each model and its part and keeping what the text claims as the author's decision, and its tag vocabulary grades the share and direction of a text's machine participation from "human_primary" through "human_directed_ai_assisted" to "collaborative_mixed".

sentences.sense: the census's question and its reading
sentences.text: The leesharks.com authorship census, whose rows are aggregators that gather many works or records and say what they hold, holds CoAuthor as an empirical comparator, under machine co-authorship and attribution and credit, for its question, "How is authorship made, named, distributed, attributed and sustained across persons, personas, collectives and machine participation, and what is lost when those relations are collapsed?", and gives it the narrower question of what a language model contributes to a writing session, read from recorded interactions, answering also how many writers, instances and sessions it holds.

sentences.sense: the census's question and its reading
sentences.text: It reads the dataset as process evidence of distributed contribution held at the session level, the persons counted and the question of whose name the text bears left outside the record as saved, and tags it as no record of named authors, no sustained literary practice and no claim of the model's authorship, and lists how a sustained named poetic practice works among what it does not answer, the study population and task setting differing.

The archive sets CoAuthor as a comparator for its own dataset export, its properties taken from its own documentation and undiscounted as self-description, and records a machine composition that compared Alexanarch with CoAuthor and other AI-writing corpora; its disambiguation matrix gives CoAuthor's object as writing sessions and its identifier as a dataset DOI or URL.

The dataset, its metadata and its survey responses can be downloaded from its site, which links the paper and the interface code and directs questions to "Mina", and the paper calls the dataset and the replay interface "publicly available".

The census, whose fetch of the home page on 1 November 2026 failed with a TLS certificate error, records the dataset as historical, whether its site and replay interface still answer as unrecorded, its geography and license as not stated, and its home page, the paper's full text and the license as unchecked; the site's pages were read the same day.

The paper that presents it, by Mina Lee, Percy Liang and Qian Yang, describes "a dataset designed for revealing GPT-3's capabilities in assisting creative and argumentative writing" and was published as a conference paper at CHI 2022 after arXiv versions of 18 and 25 January 2022. Its site gives the purpose as helping designers understand the generative capabilities of large language models by examining the same sessions from several perspectives. Writers received a prompt and a GPT-3 instance, wrote, asked for suggestions with the tab key, accepted or dismissed them, and edited in any order, every keystroke recorded with timestamps for replay. The instances, by alphaXiv's overview, were davinci at a high and a low randomness setting, and the interface code is published on GitHub. There are 830 stories by 58 writers and 615 essays by 49, on prompts from the WritingPrompts subreddit and The New York Times, averaging 418 words, with 11.8 queries a session and 72.3% of suggestions accepted. The writers were qualified crowd workers from Amazon Mechanical Turk, and the browse page lists them under short identifiers in a column headed "Human". The site reports that 72.6% of the text was written by humans and offers a tutorial for identifying the authors of sentences. By the overview's account, writers felt more ownership the more of the final text they authored (r=0.3), while editing showed no correlation with ownership. The paper claims the dataset can reveal GPT-3's contribution as a writing "collaborator" under various definitions of good collaboration, measured as equality and mutuality after Storch's work on ESL pair interaction. Reported findings include fewer errors in accepted suggestions, new named entities in 13% and 7% of them, reuse of 20% and 14% of those, length correlated with queries, and collaboration patterns that vary by writer. The paper motivates the dataset by the context-dependence and subjective interpretation of language-model capabilities, and the overview adds that it supplies supervision signals for training. The dataset, its metadata and survey responses are downloadable, and the paper calls the dataset and its replay interface publicly available. Wikipedia has no article on it; "Coauthor" redirects to Collaborative writing, two or more persons working on a text, a possible case of joint authorship; alphaXiv heads its account "AI Overview" and counts 812 citations.

L_BA.text: CoAuthor is a research dataset of human-AI collaborative writing, a released, schema-defined body of records that holds the interactions between 63 writers and four instances of GPT-3 across 1445 writing sessions in English. Its paper presents it as "a dataset designed for revealing GPT-3's capabilities in assisting creative and argumentative writing", and its site states the purpose: designers "can examine the same sessions from multiple analytical perspectives to better understand the generative capabilities of large language models". The name is the short title of the paper "CoAuthor: Designing a Human-AI Collaborative Writing Dataset for Exploring Language Model Capabilities" by Mina Lee, Percy Liang and Qian Yang, given with the affiliations Stanford University and Cornell University, submitted to arXiv on 18 January 2022, revised on 25 January 2022 and published as a conference paper at CHI 2022, in its Proceedings (DOI 10.1145/3491102.3502030). In each session a writer received a prompt and an instance of GPT-3, wrote freely, asked the model for suggestions, accepted or dismissed them, and edited the accepted suggestions or earlier text in any order. The writing took place in a text editor in which the tab key brought five suggestions, up to five in the account of the paper's overview on alphaXiv, and the code of the interface is published in a repository whose first part is "the frontend presented to the users for writing with AI". The instances are reported as GPT-3's davinci engine at two randomness settings, high (temperature 0.75, frequency penalty 1) and low (temperature 0.3, frequency penalty 0), and the dataset lists each session's randomness. Every interaction was recorded at the keystroke level with timestamps, inserting text, moving the cursor and receiving suggestions, "so that we could replay them precisely", and the dataset is published with an interface for replaying the sessions. The creative writing holds 830 stories by 58 writers and the argumentative writing 615 essays by 49 writers, written to prompts from the WritingPrompts subreddit and The New York Times, 20 prompts in all by the overview's count. Stories and essays run to 418 words, a session averages 11.8 queries, and 72.3% of suggestions were accepted. The writers were "Qualified crowd workers from Amazon Mechanical Turk". The dataset's browse page lists each session by type, prompt, randomness, "Human" and session ID, the human column holding a short identifier such as "A1198"; in its last row that column repeats the session ID. The authorship census records whose authorship the dataset keeps, and under what name, as not recorded in its saved source, which counted 63 writers without saying whether or how they are named, and lists who the writers are among what the dataset does not answer. Amazon announced that Mechanical Turk, the platform the writers were recruited from, would close on 30 September 2026, as the archive records from Turkopticon's own article. The dataset divides its text by origin, "Percentage of text written by humans: 72.6%", and its tutorials include one for "Identifying authors of sentences". In the paper as its overview reports it, writers felt stronger ownership when they authored a larger proportion of the final text (r=0.3), and the amount of editing showed no meaningful correlation with ownership, which the overview reads as text origin mattering more than editorial effort. The archive keeps apart two questions that such a share joins, whether AI played a material role in the production chain (the mediation question) and whether AI-produced language survived into the final text (the generation question), and requires no ratio of AI-generated to human-authored language. On its definition of the pristine fallacy, "'human-written' describes the author, not the distribution", and the binary of "human-written" and "AI-generated" is discussed "in ways that elide structured collaborative practice". The archive reads authorship as "an accountability structure", against certification that places AI-assisted work outside the human-authored category, and keeps responsibility for a work apart from sole origination. It states that the metadata attributing augmented-cognition outputs to human authorship attaches to legal names, that provenance is declared or erased under "the fiction of unmediated human authorship that current classifier regimes reward", and that a policy certifying human authorship by classifier runs from "detector score → authorship attribution" to career sanction without warrant at any step. The paper's headline claim is that the dataset can address GPT-3's language, ideation and collaboration capabilities and reveal its contribution as a writing "collaborator" under various definitions of good collaboration, and the census reads the model's part so framed, as contribution, recording that how authorship of a session's text is assigned is not recorded in its saved source. Collaboration is measured, in the overview's account, as equality, "The evenness of turn-taking between human and AI", and mutuality, "The level of human interaction with AI suggestions", concepts the paper adapts from Neomy Storch's 2002 study of interaction in ESL pair work. The reported findings are that accepted GPT-3 sentences carried fewer errors per word (0.033) than human-only text (0.037) and jointly made segments the fewest (0.032), that 13% of accepted suggestions in creative writing and 7% in argumentative writing introduced new named entities, of which writers reused 20% and 14%, that final length correlated with queries (r=0.42) and accepted suggestions (r=0.48), and that collaboration patterns varied across writers and held across prompts. The paper sets the dataset against a stated problem, that the capabilities of language models are "highly context-dependent" and "often subjectively interpreted", and argues that curating and analysing large interaction datasets lets the HCI community examine them more incisively and discuss their promises and pitfalls on a more principled footing. The overview adds that the dataset provides supervision signals for training language models for interactive, collaborative settings. Within the archive one co-writing study is read two ways, with a second study beside it: the Reverse Turing Test (#161) reports that writing with LLM assistance reduces lexical, syntactic and content diversity "even when the human writer retains final authorship and edits the AI's suggestions", an erratum (#1577) states that the study attributed the reduced diversity "to the model-contributed text; the human-contributed text was unaffected in that design", and the Wolf Boy paper (#855) reports that AI-assisted writing raises individual creativity and lowers the collective diversity of novel content. Under the archive's account of heteronymy, machine assistance whose contribution is not organized as a named witness role with declared provenance, and collaborative authorship in which no distinct heteronym is constituted, stand outside heteronymy, and its own machine witnesses are "named machine-witness roles imposed over specific machine substrates". The archive records machine participation in its own writing by naming each model and its part and keeping what the text claims as the author's decision, and its tag vocabulary grades the share and direction of a text's machine participation from "human_primary" through "human_directed_ai_assisted" to "collaborative_mixed". The leesharks.com authorship census, whose rows are aggregators that gather many works or records and say what they hold, holds CoAuthor as an empirical comparator, under machine co-authorship and attribution and credit, for its question, "How is authorship made, named, distributed, attributed and sustained across persons, personas, collectives and machine participation, and what is lost when those relations are collapsed?", and gives it the narrower question of what a language model contributes to a writing session, read from recorded interactions, answering also how many writers, instances and sessions it holds. It reads the dataset as process evidence of distributed contribution held at the session level, the persons counted and the question of whose name the text bears left outside the record as saved, and tags it as no record of named authors, no sustained literary practice and no claim of the model's authorship, and lists how a sustained named poetic practice works among what it does not answer, the study population and task setting differing. The archive sets CoAuthor as a comparator for its own dataset export, its properties taken from its own documentation and undiscounted as self-description, and records a machine composition that compared Alexanarch with CoAuthor and other AI-writing corpora; its disambiguation matrix gives CoAuthor's object as writing sessions and its identifier as a dataset DOI or URL. The dataset, its metadata and its survey responses can be downloaded from its site, which links the paper and the interface code and directs questions to "Mina", and the paper calls the dataset and the replay interface "publicly available". The census, whose fetch of the home page on 1 November 2026 failed with a TLS certificate error, records the dataset as historical, whether its site and replay interface still answer as unrecorded, its geography and license as not stated, and its home page, the paper's full text and the license as unchecked; the site's pages were read the same day. Wikipedia has no article on the dataset; its title "Coauthor", the common noun, redirects to Collaborative writing, which defines the homonym as a procedure in which two or more persons work together on a text and admits a case of joint authorship where more than one person creates a work in collaboration. alphaXiv carries the paper with an account it heads "AI Overview", beside an "overview generator", and counts 812 citations. Asked "CoAuthor dataset" on 1 November 2026, signed out, Google's AI Overview composed the dataset with its authors, size, composition, mechanics and access from five cards (the site, the arXiv and ACM pages, the code repository and alphaXiv), at a finer grain than the census's saved abstract and from the site the census could not read, the Capture Registry finds. The registry finds that the composition gave the writers as crowd workers recruited from a crowd platform and named none of them, divided the text by percentage into an aggregate share of human-authored text that assigns no session's text to anyone, and left out the abstract's frame of the model as "collaborator" and the dataset's purpose. The registry enters CoAuthor as an external resource, entered in the leesharks.com apparatus authorship census on 1 November 2026.
